analysis.one_liner: Sets up an official Medicare website linking seniors to vetted online pharmacies, including cheaper imported drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2000 with no cosponsors, sent to two House committees, referred to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the government hire one insurance contractor to run an official website where Medicare beneficiaries, their doctors, and their pharmacies could find approved online pharmacies. These pharmacies could import FDA-approved prescription drugs from abroad, and the site would show the five lowest prices for any drug. Online pharmacies would have to be licensed, require valid prescriptions, and protect patient information; the government could suspend or revoke pharmacies that break the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, especially those who could save by buying FDA-approved drugs from licensed online pharmacies, including lower-priced imported versions. Community pharmacies and physicians serving Medicare patients would also get a vetted channel to compare prices.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to contract with one carrier to operate an official website where Medicare beneficiaries, physicians, and pharmacies can find qualified Internet pharmacies to buy safe domestic and international prescription drugs.
Requires the website to post the five lowest prices for a requested drug, including brand and generic equivalents, so beneficiaries can comparison shop.
Allows qualified Internet pharmacies a federal waiver to import FDA-approved prescription drugs into the United States, opening a legal path to lower-priced drugs from abroad.

Sets qualification standards for participating online pharmacies: state pharmacy licensing, valid prescriptions only, posted identity and contact information, and privacy protections for beneficiary information.
Gives the Secretary enforcement tools to suspend or revoke an online pharmacy's waiver, with criminal penalties for importations after revocation.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would face new price competition from legal importation of their own FDA-approved drugs sold cheaper abroad, and from posted price comparisons. The participating carrier and online pharmacies bear administrative and enforcement fees, which the bill expects to recover by charging pharmacies fees to use the site; those costs could pass through to drug prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on a single government-contracted carrier to screen and oversee online pharmacies selling imported drugs; critics of drug importation have long argued that foreign-sourced medicines are harder to guarantee as authentic and safely handled, and the bill addresses safety through licensing and screening standards rather than a guarantee.

The carrier recovers its administrative costs by assessing fees on the Internet pharmacies that use the site, and the Secretary collects a separate enforcement fee, costs that could ultimately be reflected in the prices beneficiaries pay.

The website is limited to identifying qualified Internet pharmacies rather than negotiating drug prices directly, so any savings depend on competition among the pharmacies the carrier chooses to link.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries without drug coverage in 2000, who paid retail prices at the pharmacy counter, the bill offered a direct way to comparison shop and legally buy the same FDA-approved drugs at lower foreign prices, with licensing, prescription, and privacy rules to screen out rogue sellers. The main risks are the difficulty of guaranteeing the safety of imported medicines through a contractor-run screening system and the pass-through of administrative fees; on balance the consumer benefit is the bill's clear purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2000 with no cosponsors and referred to the Commerce (Energy and Commerce) and Ways and Means Committees; a subcommittee got it in October, and the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on September 7, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress.
It was referred to the Committee on Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
On October 19, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action followed before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, pharmaceutical manufacturers kept their protection against price competition from legal drug importation, and Medicare beneficiaries continued paying U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs. Online and brick-and-mortar pharmacies also faced no new federal licensing and fee regime.

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on September 7, 2000.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: Legal importation of FDA-approved drugs and posted price comparisons would expose U.S. prices to competition from cheaper sales of the same drugs abroad. Manufacturers kept that protection because the bill never got a vote.

Qualified online pharmacies would gain a government-vetted sales channel to Medicare beneficiaries, but would have to meet licensing, prescription, and disclosure rules and pay fees to the site's carrier and enforcement fees to the Secretary.
One carrier would win an exclusive federal contract to operate the official website and could charge participating pharmacies fees to recover its costs.
Pharmacies serving Medicare patients could use the site to find lower-priced suppliers, but legal imported drugs sold through online pharmacies would compete with their dispensing business.
